doc.title: Ed Polcer interviewed by Monk Rowe, Tarrytown, New York, October 31, 1998

title: What he thinks about when improvising: collective improvisation
summary: He describes listening and leaving space in ensemble playing, praising Peplowski and Tom Artin, and how he builds continuity in solos.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Earlier on you made a statement about — when you were talking about the xylophone — people ask what are you thinking about when you’re improvising. You said not much. Can we talk about that for a moment? Because I agree with your statement about how helpful it is to be able to see the chords.
It works in your subconscious someplace. I don’t know. What do I think about?

Well first, one of the things I like most about classic jazz which is a nice all around handle that I can put on my spectrum let’s say of jazz, is collective improvisation, which has gone down the tubes to a large degree in recent years. There’s been much more prevalent solo playing. You get a lot of younger players and they don’t even get into this

thing of listening to the other horns. I mean I find myself in situations where the trombonist or the clarinetist or the saxophone are really playing solos even while you’re playing an ensemble chorus. I think what I want to say is what goes through my mind is I do feel the interaction of the other players and I love the interaction with other horn players. But in order to do that you’ve got to leave spaces and listen to what the other guy is doing. It’s almost like playing a duet or a trio. It’s one of the beauties of collective improvisation. So what is going through my mind is I am listening to the others players, and I’m saying Oh now the rhythm section just decided to give me a Charleston beat, okay, I’m going to shift my beat and do this, I’m going to lay a few notes down, I’m going to hear what the clarinet or the sax is going to give me back. This is during the ensemble part of the playing. And there are very few players who really are tuned into ensemble playing. Ken Peplowski is marvelous. He believes in leaving a lot of space. The space is important in ensemble playing. Tom Artin is wonderful with his putting the bottom in. He knows when to go up to the upper range on the trombone. Some of it is familiarity from working together in that case. But still, I love the collective thing. And when I am playing a solo, I don’t know what I’m thinking of. I might have had some classical music in the back of my head that I listened to earlier that day, some beautiful melody. I try to create in my solos some kind of continuity. I don’t think consciously of leading the audience into my solos but I think that is the bottom line. I’ve had several people say we love how you’re weaving in your solos, we can follow you. And maybe in a way I’ve kept simpler, I’ve kept my style simpler rather than fast, rapid technique, I choose to play simpler.
